title: Explain Inventory Management without starting from movement codes
prompt: Explain how you read an inventory event from business purpose to material document, stock state, financial effect, warehouse ownership, and reconciliation.
expected_points: business event before movement type
reference document or business authority
movement semantics
stock dimensions such as plant, storage location and stock type
special stock or batch context where relevant
valuation and accounting boundary
IM versus EWM ownership
material document and reversal/reconciliation evidence
follow_up_questions: What does a movement type control beyond quantity?
Why can total stock be correct while the next process still cannot use it?
red_flags: only lists movement type numbers
treats all stock as one quantity
does not separate ERP inventory state from EWM warehouse execution

title: Stock exists but is not usable
prompt: A material shows sufficient plant stock, but production cannot consume the required quantity. How do you diagnose the inventory state before changing stock manually?
expected_points: confirm material, plant, requirement date and consuming process
break stock down by storage location and stock type
check special-stock ownership, batch or valuation segment where relevant
check reservation or requirement context
trace the material document that created the quantity
check QM disposition or EWM location if relevant
correct the owning state transition rather than posting a blind transfer
follow_up_questions: How is this different from an ATP problem?
What changes if the quantity is in quality inspection stock?
red_flags: uses total plant stock as proof of availability
posts an unrestricted transfer immediately
ignores special stock and warehouse context

title: Stock left the issuing location but has not arrived
prompt: During an internal stock movement, issuing stock decreases but the receiving location has no unrestricted stock. Trace the possible designed states before calling the quantity missing.
expected_points: identify transfer posting versus stock transfer
identify one-step versus two-step process
trace stock in transfer or transit where designed
read issuing and receiving material documents
check receiving location and expected second posting
check STO, delivery or EWM involvement when applicable
complete or reverse the original chain instead of creating an unrelated receipt
follow_up_questions: When does a storage-location transfer have accounting impact?
Why would a business choose a two-step transfer?
red_flags: creates a new goods receipt without tracing the issue
calls transit stock lost stock
does not distinguish logical transfer posting from physical stock transfer

title: Physical inventory difference is posted every month
prompt: A fast-moving storage location repeatedly shows negative physical inventory differences. Posting the differences makes book stock correct each month. What would a Lead do next?
expected_points: separate control completion from root-cause elimination
compare count time with goods-movement and warehouse timestamps
check open or delayed movements
segment differences by material, location, shift, unit, batch or process
reconcile ERP and EWM when applicable
understand accounting impact of differences
define corrective ownership and a measurable recurrence check
follow_up_questions: What evidence would show a timing problem instead of theft or damage?
Why is a successful difference posting not proof that the process is fixed?
red_flags: treats monthly adjustment as normal closure
changes book stock before validating count scope
does not investigate warehouse/process timing

title: Receipt is posted but stock is still not available
prompt: A supplier delivery is visible in PO history, but unrestricted stock did not increase and the business asks for a manual 101. Trace the designed receipt states before changing stock.
expected_points: identify whether the original receipt was 103 nonvaluated GR blocked stock or 107 valuated GR blocked stock
for 103 explain that release with 105 creates the normal stock and valuation update
for 107 explain that value is already posted at origin acceptance and 109 records warehouse arrival
check PO history and material document before posting anything else
use 124 for a rejected quantity from nonvaluated GR blocked stock where appropriate
reverse the original wrong posting instead of adding a compensating 101
follow_up_questions: What is the main difference between 103/105 and 107/109?
red_flags: posts a second 101 immediately
treats all blocked stock as the same state
ignores valuation and invoice timing

title: Choose the right plant-to-plant transfer model
prompt: Two plants need regular replenishment. The business wants visibility while material is moving and wants MRP at the receiving plant to see the expected receipt. Compare one-step transfer, two-step transfer, and a Stock Transport Order.
expected_points: 301 one-step is simplest but has no transit phase
303/305 two-step creates stock in transfer and separates removal from putaway
an STO provides purchasing-document control, PO history and receiving-plant planning
STO without delivery typically uses 351 goods issue and 101 goods receipt
distinguish stock in transfer from stock in transit
explain FI impact when valuation areas differ and cross-company-code clearing when company codes differ
choose based on process control and visibility rather than movement-code familiarity
follow_up_questions: When does valuation occur in a two-step plant transfer?
Why is an STO stronger than a direct 303/305 process for recurring replenishment?
red_flags: chooses 301 only because it is fewer steps
calls stock in transfer and stock in transit the same thing
ignores MRP and accounting effects

title: Same material, different ownership
prompt: A warehouse holds supplier consignment stock, company-owned components at a subcontractor, and normal own stock. Explain why physical location alone is not enough to decide valuation or liability.
expected_points: vendor consignment uses special stock K and remains supplier-owned while stored at the company
consignment receipt is nonvaluated and liability arises at withdrawal or transfer to own stock
411 K transfers consignment into own stock and settlement clears liabilities
subcontracting components use special stock O and remain company-owned and valuated at the supplier
541 can provide components to the subcontractor and finished-product GR consumes components
start diagnosis with ownership and special-stock indicator before changing stock
follow_up_questions: What business event creates the liability in consignment?
Why is subcontracting stock O valuated while consignment K is not?
red_flags: treats both external-location scenarios as supplier-owned
assumes warehouse location defines ownership
uses normal unrestricted stock postings to correct special stock

title: Book stock exists but the reservation still reports shortage
prompt: There are 100 pieces in unrestricted stock, but a new reservation or goods issue reports that the requested quantity is not available. How do you diagnose static versus dynamic availability before changing stock?
expected_points: static availability checks the physical stock segment affected by the movement
dynamic availability also considers planned receipts and issues from the MRP view
check existing reservations and requirement dates
check the relevant checking group, checking rule and scope
consider the replenishment lead-time or check horizon when it is part of the rule
check special stock and storage-location scope
use missing-parts logic at goods receipt when the incoming quantity covers an uncovered requirement
do not enable negative stock as a shortcut for a planning or reservation problem
follow_up_questions: Why can book stock be 100 while only 50 is dynamically available?
When is negative stock a legitimate temporary exception?
red_flags: uses book stock as the only evidence
deletes reservations without checking ownership
enables negative stock to silence the error
